title: Kamala
focus: entering the city and learning love

teacherSummary.text: Siddhartha dreams of Govinda becoming a woman, crosses a river with a kind ferryman (Vasudeva) who predicts his return, and reaches a city where he sees the beautiful courtesan Kamala. She tells him he needs fine clothes, shoes and money; he learns quickly and, through her, gains a position with the merchant Kamaswami. Kamala becomes his teacher in love.

I can fast” slowly and put it in my own words: Siddhartha's three skills: everything his ascetic life gave him, offered as currency in the city. Next, craft. The word “think” stands out; I ask why the writer chose it over a plainer word. Then, effect. What does this reveal about the speaker? In this chapter: Siddhartha enters the world: the ferryman Vasudeva carries him across for nothing; a young village woman offers herself and he declines; he sees the courtesan Kamala and decides she will be his teacher of love.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the chapter for characterization, foreshadowing (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this chapter suggest about entering the city and learning love? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Kamala develops the idea of entering the city and learning love. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim. (You are reading the English translation by Gunther Olesch, Anke Dreher, Amy Coulter, Stefan Langer and Semyon Chaichenets, so word-choice evidence is the translators' English.)) Exemplar: Vasudeva's words at the river foreshadow that Siddhartha's journey into the world is a detour that will lead back. When the text says “This too, I have learned from the river: everything is coming back” (Kamala, paragraph 11), it shows this directly. The ferryman says "This too, I have learned from the river: everything is coming back! You too, Samana, will come back," naming the river as his teacher and predicting Siddhartha's return long before it happens.
